Orbiter (~1230 kg dry, 11 instruments) + Philae descent lander (~100 kg, 10 instruments). Three Earth + one Mars gravity assist, 957 days of deep-space hibernation 2011–2014.

© ESA / Rosetta / NavCam / OSIRIS — CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO mission imagery. Rosetta launched 2004-03-02 from Kourou on a 10-year cruise that included Earth gravity assists (2005-03-04, 2007-11-13, 2009-11-13) and a Mars flyby (2007-02-25), with main-belt asteroid encounters at 2867 Šteins (2008-09-05) and 21 Lutetia (2010-07-10). The spacecraft hibernated 2011-06 to 2014-01 (deep-space radio silence, beyond solar-array operating range), then woke and rendezvoused with comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko 2014-08-06 — the first spacecraft ever to enter orbit around a comet. Philae detached 2014-11-12 and bounced into the shadow of a cliff after harpoon failure; it returned ~64 hours of science before its primary battery drained. Rosetta itself observed 67P through perihelion (2015-08-13) and into outbound dust decay before a controlled descent to the surface on 2016-09-30 ended the mission. Key discoveries: organics + glycine + phosphorus in comet coma; 67P's initially-measured D/H ratio (≈3× terrestrial) argued against Jupiter-family comets as Earth's water source — a result a 2024 re-analysis has since called into question after finding a measurement error; first close-up imaging of cometary outgassing geometry.
Altwegg et al. (2015) — D/H ratio in 67P comet water (Science 347)
The Planetary Society — Rosetta mission retrospective

Kourou, French Guiana, 2004-03-02. ESA's flagship cometary mission, designed to rendezvous with comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko during its 2014–2016 inner-solar-system passage. The launch slipped 13 months from a January 2003 window targeting comet 46P/Wirtanen — a fault in Ariane 5 forced re-planning to the alternative comet.
Closest approach 1,955 km on 2005-03-04. First of four gravity assists in the cruise plan — the chemical engine alone can't reach 67P's aphelion at 5.7 AU.

Closest approach 250 km above the Martian surface on 2007-02-25 — only 15 minutes inside Mars's eclipse. The spacecraft was put into hibernation mode during the brief eclipse to conserve power, then commanded back to operation immediately on emergence.
Closest approach 5,301 km on 2007-11-13. Briefly mistaken for a near-Earth asteroid (designated 2007 VN84) before observers realised it was Rosetta heading out.

Closest approach 800 km from main-belt asteroid 2867 Steins on 2008-09-05. Steins's diamond-shaped 6 km E-type body provided the first close-up confirmation of an enstatite-chondrite parent body's surface morphology.
Final Earth flyby on 2009-11-13, closest approach 2,481 km. The boost takes Rosetta out to the aphelion needed to match 67P's orbit, after which the spacecraft entered deep-space hibernation.

Closest approach 3,162 km from main-belt asteroid 21 Lutetia on 2010-07-10. At ~120 km mean diameter, Lutetia is the largest asteroid ever visited at close range; the M-type spectrum + high density suggested a metal-rich differentiated body.

Arrived at comet 67P on 2014-08-06 — the first spacecraft to rendezvous with a comet (matching velocities, not just flying past). Released Philae lander on 2014-11-12; Philae bounced twice in the comet's ~10⁻⁴ g gravity but returned 64 hours of surface data. Rosetta continued orbiting 67P through perihelion in 2015, ended on 2016-09-30 with a controlled descent to the comet's surface.
First spacecraft to orbit a comet — and to land on one (Philae, 2014-11-12)

ESA's flagship comet-rendezvous mission. After a 10-year cruise that wove three Earth assists, a Mars assist, two asteroid flybys, and 957 days of deep-space hibernation, Rosetta caught up with comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko in August 2014 and orbited it for over two years through perihelion and out the back side. The Philae lander reached 67P's surface 2014-11-12 — the first soft landing on a comet — and returned ~64 hours of science after a harpoon failure left it in the shadow of a cliff. Rosetta itself ended the mission with a controlled descent to 67P's surface on 2016-09-30. Key results: organic molecules and glycine in the coma; 67P's initially-measured D/H ratio (≈3× terrestrial) argued against Jupiter-family comets as Earth's water source — a result a 2024 re-analysis has since called into question after finding a measurement error; the first detailed maps of comet outgassing geometry.
Ariane 5G+ lifts Rosetta from Kourou for the 10-year cruise to comet 67P.
First of three Earth gravity assists to build velocity for the comet rendezvous.
Single Mars gravity assist + first close imagery of Phobos and Mars at 250 km.
First-ever close-up of an E-type asteroid.
~120 km flyby of one of the largest main-belt asteroids ever observed close-up.
Orbit insertion around comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. Philae lands 2014-11-12.
